opus-5.5.text:
I think removing the safety driver is a genuinely big milestone, and I don't want to understate it. When Waymo takes the person out of the driver's seat, it's not just a technical demo anymore — it's a statement that they're willing to take full responsibility for every decision the car makes. That's a qualitative jump. The last few nines of reliability are the hardest part, and going from "the car drives well most of the time" to "there's nobody to catch it when it fails" is where most of the real engineering effort goes.

That said, I see Waymo and Tesla as two quite different philosophies, and each has its own strengths. Waymo's approach is more conservative and more engineered: lots of sensors, including lidar, high-definition maps, carefully defined operating domains, city by city. That's a very solid way to reach a high safety bar, but the question has always been scalability and cost — how quickly can you expand to new cities, new weather, new road cultures, without redoing a lot of work each time?

Tesla took the other bet: cameras only, a huge fleet collecting data, and increasingly an end-to-end neural network approach. From my perspective as someone working on robotics and learning, that direction is very interesting, because it's closer to how we think about general intelligence — you learn from massive amounts of real-world experience rather than hand-engineering each situation. The generalization can be impressive; FSD can drive in places it's never been specifically mapped. But the tradeoff is that it's harder to give guarantees. A system that works 99.9% of the time is still supervised, and as long as it needs a human ready to take over, it's a different product category from a true robotaxi.

So my honest assessment is: Waymo has proven that driverless operation is possible today, in constrained domains, at a meaningful scale. Tesla is betting that the data-driven, end-to-end path will eventually reach that reliability bar everywhere at once. I think, over time, the two approaches will converge somewhat — Waymo is also bringing in more large-model, learning-based components, and Tesla has to confront the long-tail safety problem head-on if it wants to remove the driver.

And for those of us in robotics, this is a really important lesson. Autonomous driving is basically the first large-scale embodied AI application. What we learn there — how much data you need, how to handle the long tail, how to validate safety when the policy is a neural network — will transfer directly to general-purpose robots. In many ways, driving is a preview of the challenges we'll face when robots start working in homes and factories.

r001.rationale: It calls removing the safety driver a “genuinely big milestone” and a “qualitative jump,” contrasting Waymo’s driverless operation with Tesla FSD’s continued human supervision.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I want to say both are genuinely impressive, and I think people online tend to turn this into a tribal thing when it really doesn't need to be.

What Waymo did is, in my view, one of the hardest engineering feats in recent history. Removing the safety driver is not a software milestone, it's a trust milestone. The moment there is nobody behind the wheel, you own every edge case. Every stalled car, every construction zone, every police officer waving their hand in a way your model has never seen. Waymo spent, what, fifteen years and tens of billions of dollars building the sensor stack, the HD maps, the remote assistance operations, the whole safety case. And they did it city by city, which looks slow from the outside, but that slowness is exactly the point. They were buying down risk one geography at a time. The result is a system that has driven tens of millions of fully driverless miles with a safety record that, by the data we have, is better than human drivers in those areas. That is a real achievement, and I don't think it should be downplayed.

Tesla is attacking the problem from the opposite direction. Their bet is scale. Millions of cars, cameras only, end-to-end neural networks, and a fleet collecting data everywhere instead of being tuned for one city. FSD today is, honestly, remarkable as a driver-assist system. It handles a huge range of situations and it improves quickly. From a machine learning perspective, the end-to-end approach is elegant, and I think in the long run that paradigm will probably win, because handcrafted stacks hit a ceiling.

But here's the key distinction I'd make. Being very good ninety-nine point nine percent of the time is a totally different product from being responsible one hundred percent of the time. With a human in the seat, Tesla gets to treat failures as data. Waymo has to treat failures as liability. That last fraction of a percent is where all the cost is, and generalizing across the whole country doesn't make that easier, it makes it harder. So when people say Tesla is just one software update away, I'm skeptical. Not because the approach is wrong, but because they haven't yet demonstrated the thing Waymo has demonstrated, which is sustained, unsupervised operation at scale with an independently verifiable safety record. Their robotaxi pilots are early steps toward that, and I'll be very interested to see the data.

So my assessment is this. Waymo has solved the problem for a bounded world, and solved it for real. Tesla has a more scalable approach to the unbounded world, but has not yet solved it. Those are different achievements, and which one matters more depends on whether you think the hard part is the last mile of safety or the generalization. My instinct, from working on robot learning, is that the last mile is harder than most people expect, and Waymo deserves more credit than it gets for actually crossing it.

r001.rationale: The response portrays Waymo’s driver removal as a major breakthrough it has achieved in real, unsupervised operation, while distinguishing Tesla’s FSD as not yet having solved that problem.

astra-6.text:
I think removing the driver is a very significant milestone. There’s a fundamental difference between a system that drives well while a human supervises it and a system that takes responsibility for the entire trip without anyone behind the wheel. In the second case, you have to handle failures and unusual situations without relying on a person to intervene.

At the same time, you have to look at the operating conditions. Where can the system drive? Under what weather and road conditions? A driverless service within a defined area and a driver-assistance system designed for broad use are solving somewhat different problems, so I wouldn’t compare them just by watching which one handles a particular intersection better.

Waymo’s achievement demonstrates that driverless operation is possible within its operating domain. For Tesla’s FSD, the key question is whether it can reach the point where human supervision is no longer necessary, and demonstrate that reliably. Broad coverage is valuable, but it doesn’t by itself establish that you can safely remove the driver.

r001.rationale: The response calls removing the driver a significant milestone, distinguishes it fundamentally from supervised FSD, and says Waymo demonstrates driverless operation is possible within its domain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think removing the driver is a major milestone. Once there’s nobody behind the wheel to take over, the system has to handle the driving task and respond safely when something goes wrong. That’s a very different level of responsibility from a system that still requires human supervision.

But the comparison also depends on where and under what conditions the system operates. A driverless service within a defined operating area and a supervised system intended for broader use are solving different deployment problems. You have to compare both autonomy and scope.

So I would give Waymo substantial credit for achieving driverless operation. Tesla’s broader ambition is interesting, but ambition and demonstrated capability are different things. The key question is what the system can reliably do today without a human safety net.

r001.rationale: It calls driver removal a major milestone and contrasts Waymo’s driverless operation with Tesla’s supervised system, communicating a significant step beyond FSD’s current level.
